“Zhou Shun, right?” I stand at the doorway of grid eleven, Yi section, in the corridor cabin, a steaming teacup in my hand. “The fog belt tossed things around badly last night. I heard you didn’t sleep soundly—this cup of ginger tea was saved especially for you.”

Third watch. I went to the stern first.
The wax seal on Sparrow No. 12 lay smooth and snug; the tail-tip of the sparrow-feather pattern leaned half a fraction to the left. I had pressed that pattern with my own hands—off by even a hair, and I would know. But I crouched down, looked at the suspension line by starlight, then pressed my palm against the ship’s side to feel the angle at which it took the wind.
The stern had sunk by a little less than half a finger.
The seal was real; the weight was false. Someone had gone through that door, come out, and sealed it back exactly as before. No matter how lifelike the lacquerwork was, the ship would not lie for anyone. All the extra weight was pressing down on the stern, like a scale that refused to speak, tilting only to one side.
So I carried a second cup of ginger tea and stood again before Door Yi-11. I repeated that sentence exactly as before, without changing a single word. If I changed it, I would be the one who looked guilty.
The lamp inside was lit. The door opened neither quickly nor slowly—the way it does for someone who has been waiting a long time.
“Chief Holdmaster’s tea—one cup is protocol, two cups means there’s business.” Zhou Shun stepped aside. On the small table sat a brass kettle, the charcoal sparks not yet quite extinguished. “The water—I’ve kept it warm for two incense sticks. You give me two cups, I return one. That doesn’t count as discourtesy.”
He poured the tea. His wrist rested on a cloth towel, the spout held neither high nor low, seven-tenths full, not a drop spilled. I watched his hands—the craft of serving people was something I recognized, but what mattered more than craft was in the cracks beneath the nails.
“Greener by another line than yesterday.” I lifted his hand under the lamp. “The kind of green that soap pods can’t wash off. Tonight, did your hands go in there or not?”
“I went to identify the door.” This time he did not circle around it. “The door was opened by someone else.”
“Who.”
“I don’t know the name.” He pushed the tea in front of me. “They took the outer hull, not the corridor. No lamp. Their toes hooked into the cable groove, climbing onto the ship’s side from that broken ladder below the waterline. From that stretch of sentry post, you can’t see it.”
A chill ran down the back of my neck. Outer hull, cable groove, broken ladder—this was not a sailor’s skill. It was a cable worker’s skill, the kind only feet that had earned their keep half a lifetime on ship hulls could use to hold a cable groove. There were not many such hands under heaven; they had come from the same mold as mine.
“Someone without a pass.” I said it word by word. Passes, faces, mud on the soles of shoes—these eyes of mine had watched them for twenty years. Today, someone had not passed through them.
“When Luoxia docks, customs will receive an anonymous notice of cargo weight discrepancy.” Zhou Shun’s voice clung to the steam of the tea. “The weight that comes up short on the scale will need someone to answer for it. The seal was sealed by Chief Holdmaster’s own hands.”
“What was originally in the hold—you and I need not say it out loud. Saying it benefits no one.” I stared at him. “Just answer me this: what was added afterward—was it that wet raw slag from the docks?”
He was silent for two breaths. “Yes. Three pieces, wrapped in oilcloth, placed in... the place they should least have been placed.”
The place they should least have been placed. The place next to that layer of mine. Raw slag has an unsettled nature; with the jolting left before tomorrow morning, no one would dare guarantee anything for it. This was no longer setting a trap. This was handing a tinder tube into a powder magazine—and the person setting the trap was on the ship too.
“Does your employer’s abacus include you as one of its beads?” I asked. “If the ship blows up, are you sleeping above or below?”
He held the cold tea in both hands. After a long while, he said the most human sentence I heard that night: “I’ve carried tea trays for half my life. I know what happens when tea goes cold. If the ship really capsizes, the account books won’t record a single word for me.”
“Enough.” I rose. I had not touched his cup of tea, but his words—I accepted them. “Take a message to your employer: that favor from ten years ago, I acknowledge the principal; the interest, I will weigh. If he wants to collect an entire ship of lives with principal and interest together, he has found the wrong debtor.”
Leaving the corridor cabin, I first detoured to the kitchen and picked up a small bag of finely sifted furnace ash. Before daybreak, Mute Uncle and I would make a trip along the outer hull: the cable groove, the broken ladder, the section below the waterline—wherever those hands could have gripped, we would scatter a layer of ash. Furnace ash does not recognize faces; it recognizes handprints.
As for the three extra oilcloth-wrapped pieces at the stern, before daybreak, they had to leave my ship.
Passing the east corridor, the speckled chicken was sleeping soundly, and the pigeon had buried its head under its wing. I lightened my steps. Beneath the wind window, anything may be thrown out—this rule is older than Xuanhe’s accounts, harder than Steward Shen’s abacus.

“Zhou Shun, right?” I stand at the doorway of grid eleven, Yi section, in the corridor cabin, a steaming teacup in my hand. “The fog belt tossed things around badly last night. I heard you didn’t sleep soundly—this cup of ginger tea was saved especially for you.”

The third cup of ginger tea was one I simmered over the charcoal embers of the fourth watch.
Before I simmered the tea, the job in hold three had already been done. Sparrow No. 12, my own sealing wax, the seal opened by my own hand. Three bundles of wetborn residue wrapped in oilcloth, set in a wicked spot, pressed tight against the double skin—shift them half an inch more, and tonight it would not have been my turn to squat by the charcoal stove drinking tea. I invited them out one by one with both hands. Even through the oilcloth, the cold still drilled along my palms into the seams of my bones. I pressed them into an old water jar half-filled with fine sand, bound it with three hemp ropes, the knots pulled into dead knots—the first kind of knot I learned at Yun Harbor when I was sixteen, the kind that tightens the harder you struggle.
The stern cargo hoist line was lowered all the way down. The instant the jar left my hand, the cable gave a “buzz” against my palm, as if shivering on someone’s behalf. The Eternal Storm had been grinding its teeth down below for several hundred years; it would not begrudge these three little pastries. Steward Shen, the weight you added—I returned it to the storm for you. The principal I acknowledge; the interest, we settle at Luoxia.
The hoist line returned true, and that half-finger of heaviness at the stern was unloaded. I resealed it with wax: Sparrow No. 13, tail tip half a fen to the left.
At the fifth watch I inspected the ash. On the thin line of ash in the cable trough, there were five toe hollows, the ball of the foot deep, the heel shallow—the gait of someone gripping the cable trough, from the same school as these two feet of mine. The ash had been scattered at the fourth watch; the prints were newer than the ash.
There were only prints going up, none coming down.
Those feet were still on my ship.
So when day was just beginning to pale, I carried the tea to the door of Yi-11 and said that line for the third time: “Zhou Shun, is it? The fog belt pitched hard last night. I heard you didn’t sleep easy. This cup of ginger tea was set aside especially for you.” The first time was etiquette. The second was probing. The third was laying my cards on the table.
The door opened. Zhou Shun stood inside, two dark hollows under his eyes. He had not slept either.
“The three things have been returned to the storm. The ship is level now.” I pushed the tea into his hands. “That anonymous slip your master sent to Luoxia—now the scales balance perfectly. He meant to accuse me, but he washed me clean first instead.”
He held the tea and did not drink.
“There are prints in the ash.” I stared into his eyes. “After the fourth watch, someone came up again. Went up, but didn’t come down. No pass, no register, not on the roll-call ledger—at the Chen hour, every person on this ship will stand under my eyes, and only he need not stand there. Tell me, what is this sort of business after?”
Zhou Shun was silent for a long time, so long that the sky outside the corridor seeped a thread of gray out of the ink.
“Chief Steward, you came up as a cableman.” At last he spoke, his voice low as water flowing beneath the planks. “Where on this ship a person can curl up and still hear the door of hold three, you know better than I do.”
“I do know.” I said. “I slept in every one of this ship’s seams when I was sixteen.”
“Then there’s no need for me to run my mouth.” He lowered his head and took a sip of tea, drinking that sip very slowly. “I’ll only throw in one line for free: those ears are even sharper than Chief Steward’s eyes. Before you move, make a commotion in the east corridor first. Chickens will do, pigeons will do. Once livestock starts crying, human ears go deaf.”
I turned to leave, and behind me he softly added half a sentence, as if talking to himself: “At roll call in the Chen hour, I’ll be the first to arrive.”
This was the first time he had handed me anything. I accepted it.
In the east corridor, I lifted a corner of the cloth and scattered in a small half-handful of broken rice. The hour had not yet come, but the speckled chickens fluffed up first; the pigeons flapped and crashed all over the cages. Half the corridor was full of wingbeats, enough to cover footsteps for a while.
Passing the side door of hold three, Sparrow No. 13 sat neat and proper, its tail tip half a fen to the left. My pattern, my door. Mute Uncle was nailed into the shadow of the cable post; at that opening on the outer hull, even a fly would have to report its number before passing.
The stern sail-and-cable room. The lamp was turned low, and the shadows of the cable reels piled layer upon layer, like old accounts coiled there for twenty years. Beneath the second tier of cable reels was that seam: a person could curl into it, spine pressed to the planks, and not a single sound of the door within three steps overhead would escape the ears. Back then, when I was hiding from the foreman, I slept there for an entire winter.
The curled edge of the old canvas that blocked the cables had lifted half an inch higher than I remembered.
I set the lamp on top of the cable reel and wrapped half a loop of fine cord around my right wrist. Not to tie anyone up; when there is rope at hand, my heart steadies.
“Come out.” I spoke to the black mass behind the canvas, my voice level as a weighing scale. “The ginger tea on the stove is still warm. When I invite someone to tea, I invite them only once. The second time, it won’t be me doing the inviting.”

“Come out.” I speak to the clump of black behind the canvas, keeping my voice as level as a platform scale. “The ginger tea on the stove is still warm. When I invite someone to tea, I invite them only once. The second time, it won't be me doing the inviting.”

Behind the canvas, it was quiet for three breaths.
Then a hand came out first.
It was not the way someone reaches out to surrender. Five fingers spread, first feeling for the deck, then shedding force; the man slid out close against the ship’s planking, his back never leaving the wood, like a length of cable that had come alive on its own. In all of Yun Harbor, there were only a handful who could get out of a tight gap like that, all of them people who made their living by tying their lives to the outside of a hull.
He stood up straight. Half a head shorter than me, about fifty, in a gray cloth short jacket and trousers, reeking of tung oil mixed with rainwater gone sour. Hanging outside the ship’s side for half the night was the only way to pick up that smell.
Both hands spread open, palms toward me, the web between thumb and forefinger turned upward. When cablemen meet cablemen, showing the tiger’s mouth is the old rule: no weapon in hand.
I lifted the lamp half an inch. The first thing I looked at was not his face, but his right hand. The index finger was missing one joint; the stump was rounded and blunt, an old wound.
"Gecko."
I had not said that name in ten years, but it was still familiar the moment I called it out. The best hand in the Yun Harbor Cable Gang at climbing hulls, a man who dared step along wet cables on the outer rail in storm weather. I entered the gang at sixteen; he was the first one who taught me to tie knots. The dead knot, the one that tightens the more you struggle—the one I used last night to tie down the water jars was still his method.
"Little Wanxing." He recognized me too, his voice as hoarse as soaked hemp. "You’ve become chief hold officer."
I did not untie the fine cord around his wrist. Old rules were old rules; tonight’s business was tonight’s business.
"Where are the things?" He did not look at me, but at the lamp atop the cable reel. "Three pieces. I came to collect them."
"One step late. At the third watch I went in and collected them myself. At the fourth watch, I fed them to the storm."
His shoulders sagged by an inch. Not the slackness of being caught, but the slackness of setting down a burden.
"That’s good." He said it twice. "That’s good."
"Steward Shen sent you to plant them."
He did not answer that, but asked instead, "Is Uncle Ya still on the ship?"
"He is."
"That night at the berth, he was the one who hauled me out of the water." He stared at his own hands. "The two anchor cables you cut—one end was tied to the cargo, the other to me. When the cable snapped, I went into the water with it. The fire didn’t climb onto the ship, but I nearly fed myself to the harbor bottom."
The lampwick trembled. The rain from that night ten years ago splashed back over the nape of my neck with a hiss. When I cut the cable, the other end had been dragging heavy; I thought it was tied to cargo.
"The job was explained like this: add weight, press down the stern, make Luoxia Customs’ scales fail to match, get the chief hold officer dragged into a lawsuit, and the merchant guild switches to another ship for the route." He spoke very slowly. "Only after I got onto the outer rail did I start to taste it out. Raw slag laid against the lining in the sandwich layer—that wasn’t rigging a scale. That was setting off a charge. If the ship really bucked itself apart, what failed to match the scales would be more than cargo."
"I leveled the scales." I stared at him. "Talk about that letter."
"I didn’t deliver the letter, and neither did Zhou Shun. The letter set out three days earlier than the ship, by the merchant guild’s pigeon." For the first time, he looked me squarely in the eye. "What it wrote wasn’t the weight. It was the place. Hold Three, the interlayer, which compartment. I’m afraid the customs seals were cut and ready long ago, just waiting for the ship to dock."
The fleck of blue-gray in the pocket against my chest felt cold, as if another layer of ice had formed over it. I had leveled the scales, changed the seals, but the place was fixed. Once the hold was opened and they counted compartment by compartment, that piece of my "debt repayment" would be evidence nailed dead in place.
"One more thing." His voice dropped until only breath was left. "The sum Steward Shen paid for you ten years ago, when it passed through his hands, the fire in the back alley of Danhang had not yet started."
The hand with which I held the lamp stayed steady. The account book in my chest flipped with a crash all the way back to its bottom page. The fire had not yet started, but the money was already prepared. At the berth, I cut the cable to save people and believed I had incurred a favor as vast as heaven—so that fire, that sum of money, and this favor were all of a piece. A hook with its eye already bored, waiting for this fish to grow to a weight that could drag a net.
"What do you have to make me believe you?"
"Nothing." He answered bluntly. "Believe it or not, you’ll see at Luoxia Dock. All I know is that this life belongs to the Cable Gang. That path along the outer rail—no one but me can take it. Before dusk, if anyone comes up, they have to get past me first."
The edge of the sky was turning gray. From the far end of the corridor, A’Gui’s loud voice began in the distance; the roll-call line was gathering.
I untied the fine cord from his wrist and wound it back around the cable post. "Wherever you climbed up from, guard that place for me. From this moment on, that path along the outer rail is your post. Don’t guard it for Steward Shen; guard it for this ship. Uncle Ya knows your face, and I know your knots."
He froze for a moment, then pulled a short length of cord from his waist, tied a dead knot with one hand, and offered it over with both hands. The break was neat; the more it was pulled, the tighter it became. The rule of the Cable Gang was to recognize knots, not words.
"You came out the first time you were invited," I lifted my chin toward the galley, "the half-kettle of ginger tea on the stove is still warm. Go pour it yourself. After you drink, take your post."
When I went out, Uncle Ya was standing in the shadow of the cable post. He signed the character "old" at me, then pressed his own chest. Old people, old accounts. Tonight, they had all been turned out into the sun.
The clapper for the chen hour sounded. The first one standing in place under the corridor was indeed Zhou Shun, his waist bent in the same old place, but his eyes kept darting toward the stern. I picked up the register and walked toward the ladder mouth, pretending I had not seen.
The little bit of stuff in Hold Three had to have somewhere to go before Luoxia. If the storm could swallow three pieces of raw slag, it could also swallow an entire portion of "favor." But before I fed it down, I first had to make one thing clear—
Who, exactly, lit that fire ten years ago?
At dusk, on the outer rail, what kind of people would come down that path, and how many? I turned the lampwick brighter and waited to see.
“Gecko, the wind is strong outside the hull; is that severed finger of yours still afraid of the cold?”

The great inspection at chen hour was calmer than everyone had expected.
Four holds—I opened them one by one. Mine Hold No. 1 was weighed publicly; the number of stones and the weight in that bag belonging to the young mixed-crystal fellow were accurate down to the smallest fraction, and when he pressed the second handprint, he was smiling. In Hold No. 2, the lead seals on Liu Chengye’s three camphorwood chests were publicly verified; he watched from within the crowd, his shoulders loosening little by little. Miscellaneous cargo in Hold No. 4 was weighed. Hold No. 3 was the finale: the lamp was aimed at the center, and I personally broke the seal and personally weighed it—the three pieces that had come up short had already been fed to the storm last night, and the scale was as level as though nothing had ever happened. When the people filling the corridor dispersed, they whispered among themselves, all saying that “the Yunque’s rules are truly strict.” Strict rules are for people to see; a level scale is for Heaven to see.
On the roll-call register were forty-seven names, not one missing. The first to arrive was, sure enough, Zhou Shun.
In the afternoon, I carried a tea canister wrapped in a cotton cover and went down along the outer hull. The wind circled close to the ship’s side, and the white light of the sea of clouds rolled upward from below, dazzling the eyes. Gecko was fixed in the recess of the third rib, two strips of old sailcloth wrapped around the outside of his short jacket, utterly motionless, like an old callus grown onto the ship’s body.
“Gecko, the wind is strong on the outer hull. Is that severed finger of yours still afraid of the cold?”
He raised his right hand and stretched that severed finger into the wind, as if testing an old length of cable. “The part that was cut off doesn’t know
“The broken section no longer knows hot from cold,” he grinned, showing teeth yellowed by wind and sand, “but the fingers that are left still know how to grip the rope.”

“As long as you can grip it.” I unwrapped the padded cover and handed the tea canister to him. “For anyone who leaves the Cable Gang, even if his fingers are broken, his clasp must not loosen—that was the rule you taught me, taught me on my very first day up on the cables.”
Bihu took it with both hands, the hand with the broken fingers supporting it from below, as if receiving a stick of incense. Ten years on, the gang’s rules were still grown into his bones. A man with rules grown into his bones would not go too far astray. That much, I believed.
I sat down beside him in the hollow between the ribs of the hull, my legs dangling outside the gunwale. The sea of clouds rolled beneath our feet, white enough to dazzle the eyes; the wind pressed the steam from the tea flat along the deck planks. It had been ten years since we had sat like this. The last time, we were two cable workers off shift, soaking our legs in the evening wind and saying useless idle things.
The idle things had all been said. When the tea was half gone, I finally asked the question I had held in all night.
“That night, you were hanging on the cable, and I was cutting lines at the berth.” I stared at the sea of clouds. “The port records say the fire started in the back alley behind Danhang, and sparks drifted downwind to the berth. I believed that for ten years. You were hanging higher than I was; you could see more than I could. The fire you saw—where did it start?”
Bihu held the tea canister and did not move for a long time. The old canvas snapped loudly in the wind.
“From the cargo.”
Those three words hit the deck planks.
“That night I was hanging on the cable tightening the tarpaulin,” he said very slowly, as if hauling a cable up from deep water. “Hemp cable is soaked in tung oil against rot; I can tell how much by the smell. But the tarpaulin on top of that cargo pile was drenched through—far more than any anti-rot amount. I was just wondering about it when the flame licked up along the edge of the tarp. It was too fast to be fire; it was like someone was drawing it along a fuse. The fire in the back alley started only afterward. It was the fire they shouted about, to give this one on the cargo an origin.”
The two lines I cut: one end had been tied to the “cargo,” the other to him. So what had been tied there that night was a heap of oil-soaked rags, and a man whose silver had been prepared in advance, just waiting to be “compensated.”
“Before I went into the water, I glimpsed someone coming down to the dock from the cable,” he went on. “The rain was that heavy, but he carried no umbrella, and he wasn’t in a hurry. He moved right on the timing of the flame. Just as he reached the alley mouth, the fire rose. A lantern lit him for a moment. Half a silver chain slipped out of his cuff, and the pendant swung free.”
He raised the hand with the broken fingers, dipped it in tea, and drew a circle on the deck planks, adding two strokes inside.
A crane.
The account book in my chest—the page pressed at the very bottom for ten years—was torn out whole and spread beneath the sun: there was no debt. From beginning to end, there had been no debt. When I cut the lines, I saved a man; the “compensated” cargo had been set alight by the man himself; that favor was a hook. I was the fish he had reared for ten years, reared until I was heavy enough to drag a net.
I ought to have been angry. But the first thing I felt was lightness. The stone that had weighed on me for ten years had turned out to be paper pasted over a frame. The anger came behind it, pressed down, like a storm clinging to the hull, in no hurry to arrive.
“Tonight.” I poured the last mouthful of tea from the canister into the lid. “Before Luoxia makes shore, in the place where you set down the dregs, there used to be a page of accounts lying there. I tore it up with my own hands and fed it to the storm.”
“Should’ve torn it up long ago,” he said.
“Before I tore it up, I asked you about one last thing.” I fixed my eyes on him. “At dusk, who is coming aboard?”
“I don’t know his name.” He shook his head. “When Steward Shen handles business, the hand that makes the loop and the hand that gathers the line don’t meet. I only know the rule for receiving a passage. At dusk, if someone comes up from the broken ladder on the waterline, he knocks on the hull first. Two long, one short, asking for passage. It’s a Cable Gang rule: if he knocks, you have to answer.”
He paused, his broken fingers tapping three times in the air above the deck planks.
“On this outer hull, there are only three people in all who can make that climb down and back. Me. You. And one more—Hou San.” He drained the tea in the canister lid in one gulp. “If he comes up, who he’s asking passage for—I don’t dare think about it.”
Hou San. The name smashed a pit into my heart. Back then, he had the nimblest pair of hands in the gang, faster than me at tying knots, lighter than Bihu at flipping along cables. The year I left the gang, he still owed me half a jin of wine money.
“He can knock for his passage.” I stood up and wrapped the padded cover back around the canister. “The hull is mine. Two long, one short—I’ll answer. After I answer, whoever comes up will be stepping onto my deck, and once he is on my deck, he has to follow my rules.”
Bihu grinned, his yellow teeth flashing in the cloud-light. “Xiao Wanxing, your temper hasn’t changed.”
“My temper hasn’t changed. The scales have.” I patted the gunwale. “Ten years ago, I cut the lines to shield someone from the fire. Every line I cut from now on will be for everyone on this ship.”
After returning to the ship, I first made a circuit around Hold No. 3. Sparrow Thirteen lay obediently in place, the tail tip half a fraction to the left. That “favor” still lay inside the interlayer, with only a few hours of life left. Mute Uncle gestured at me from the shadow of the cable bollard: dusk, outer hull. I nodded and answered with a sign for “prepare.”
At the far end of the corridor-cabin, those who had answered roll call had each gone back to their bunks. The old carpenter was showing someone the cradle he had made for his grandson, the twining-branch pattern shining ring after ring beneath the lamp. Zhou Shun stood in the doorway of Yi-Eleven, his waist bent as usual. This time his eyes did not glance toward the stern; they flicked once toward me, quick as a mistaken brush against a lamp wick, and then he raised his hand and dusted off nonexistent ash from his sleeve.
Dusting off ash. Steward Shen’s side had probably already learned that the scales were level. News traveled faster than the ship.
Before dusk, three things: the page of accounts in the hold, tear it up; the passage along the outer hull, guard it; and prepare another cup of tea, for Hou San. If he knocks two long and one short, I will invite him to drink. If the hand that pours the tea is not clean, I cannot change this old habit of mine: however hot the tea is, I will not touch it.
The clouds flowed toward Luoxia. I turned the lamp wick half a notch brighter, sat there, and waited for dusk to come knock on my hull.
“Gecko, the wind is strong outside the hull; is that severed finger of yours still afraid of the cold?”

Before dusk, I first went to tear out that page of the account.
Hold Three, Sparrow-character No. 13, my own sealing wax, the seal opened by my own hand. In the hidden layer, that weight that had been pressed there for ten years was wrapped in three layers of oilcloth, with an old jar over it that had been filled with half a crock of fine sand; sand steadies a thing’s temper, keeps it steady on the road. I lowered the cargo sling all the way down, then let go. The Eternal Storm had had its mouth open down below for several hundred years; it was not a picky eater, nor did it ask where anything came from.
I filled the original slot in the hold with ballast stones of equal weight, stacking them neatly one by one. A ship does not ask where the weight comes from; it only asks that it be even and clean. I pressed on fresh sealing wax: Sparrow-character No. 14, the tail-tip slanting half a fen to the left. I checked the plumb line once. Straight. This time it was truly clean, clean enough to withstand anyone opening it.
When I left the hold, the edge of the sky had already begun to burn. In the direction of Luoxia Island, at the end of the cloud sea, there was a line of crimson gold. The island’s name had come from exactly that line of evening light.
Carrying the tea canister, I went down along the outer gunwale. Gecko was nailed into the old recess, like a callus grown onto the hull.
“Gecko, the wind’s strong on the outer gunwale. Is that severed bit of finger of yours still afraid of the cold?”
“That line, once at noon and once at dusk.” He took the tea canister and grinned, a flash of yellow teeth. “Chief Holdmaster is using me as a water clock.”
“A water clock doesn’t talk. You do.” I sat down beside him. “It’s dusk. That Hou San of yours—”
Before I finished speaking, a sound came from beneath the ship’s side.
Thump—thump—thump.
Two long, one short. It seeped up against the hull from below the waterline, muffled, as if striking into the seams between bones.
Gecko’s hand pressed down on the cable. I pressed down on his hand.
“By the Cable Gang’s rules, if there’s a knock, you answer it.” I pressed his hand back onto the cable. “But this is my ship’s side.” I bent my knuckles and knocked back on the hull—two long, one short. My way of answering.
The sound of someone climbing the cable came up. Light, fast, fingers hooking into the cable grooves as dense as raindrops. First came a pair of hands, five fingers spread, the web between thumb and forefinger facing upward. Then a face: thin, sharp, eyes moving faster than his head. There was frost at his temples, but those hands were still the same hands that had once tied knots faster than anyone in all Quanyun Port.
“Hou San.” I handed the words over first. “Half a jin of wine money, with ten years’ interest rolled onto it. What are you going to use to pay me back?”
He flipped himself up, squatted steady in the recess, and smiled. “One true word.”
From inside his clothes he took out a folded card and held it up in both hands. A seal was affixed at the bottom.
The Crane-character seal.
“My employer taught me to take the broken ladder and first take one look at the compartment in Hold Three.” He spoke very slowly. “If the thing was there, I was to send word back, and tomorrow morning when Customs opened the hold, contraband and culprit would match up, and this ship would change owners. If the thing wasn’t there”—he raised his eyes—“the card goes to you, and the account is calculated anew.”
“The thing isn’t there.” My voice was level. “Last night, principal and interest both, I fed it to the storm.”
He stared at me, stared for a full five breaths, and then leaned his whole body back against the ship’s side and let out a long breath, as if a cable had finally shed its strain.
“That’s good. When I took this errand, my hands were shaking.”
Gecko snorted. “Shaking and you still took it.”
“If I didn’t take it, I couldn’t get onto this ship, and I couldn’t bring the message back.”
I poured tea to seventy percent full, turned the canister lid over, and handed it to him. He came to receive it with both hands, the rim of the cup half a cun lower than my hand. I looked at his hands—the calluses at the web, the rope marks at the roots of the fingers, the spaces between the fingers clean and dry, without bluish gray. A hand that poured tea could pass my eyes. He drank it in one mouthful, fast and clean.
“Take three sentences back to your employer.” I took back the empty cup. “First, the hold is empty and the scale is level; that anonymous report of his is now a letter guaranteeing me. Second, Shopkeeper Liu’s cargo will be the first batch unloaded tomorrow morning. I will carry the first chest myself. If Customs wants to inspect it, they can inspect it in front of the whole dock; I’ll be waiting. Third—” I folded the card properly and put it into the breast pocket, placing it together with that speck of star-blue ash, “Tea, I will drink. At chen hour, have him prepare his ledger. This time, I will read the account, and he will record it.”
Hou San stood, patting the salt frost from his short jacket. “The words will be delivered. The water is deep at Luoxia Dock. Tomorrow morning, when you lower the gangway, watch your step.”
“I’ve watched my steps for twenty years,” I said. “The waterline by the broken ladder is slippery. You be careful yourself.”
He flipped down over the ship’s side and slid along the hull. Within a few breaths, there was no sound. People of the Cable Gang came and went like wind. Toward the shadow by the cable post, I signed the character for “guest,” then “go.” Mute Uncle tapped a finger on his knee, noting it down.
Gecko held the tea canister. After a long while, he came out with one sentence: “He owed you half a jin of wine money.”
“Settled today. One true word is worth ten years’ interest.”
The sky had gone completely dark. That line of crimson gold over Luoxia sank into the cloud sea, leaving only a bean-sized light in the island-top lamp tower, burning steadily in the sound of the storm grinding its teeth. The hull was level, the plumb line straight, and the snoring of forty-seven people rose and fell evenly beneath the deck planks.
I sat on the ship’s side for a while, pressing through the cloth against the two things at my chest. One speck of star-blue ash, one invitation. One page of old accounts torn out, one page of new accounts not yet written.
Tomorrow morning, at daybreak, we enter port; I will carry the first chest with my own hands. At the teahouse at chen hour, I know the hand that pours tea, and I also know the hand that ties knots.
This time, it is my turn to reach out first.
“Hou San, are those hands of yours still shaking?—If they are, that's right. It means you still remember the rules of the Cable Gang.”

We entered port at daybreak. There is not much worth writing: the ship was steady, the hoist lines true, all forty-seven people present and accounted for. Luoxia's lamp tower had shrunk to a bean of light in the morning mist, and the Yunque slid in along the tail of the wind-window and settled into its berth. Once the cable was hung, I stepped onto Luoxia's stone paving. This voyage, I could count as handed over whole.
I carried the first crate myself. Of its four hundred and thirty-one jin, I put in my share of shoulder strength. Customs came with that anonymous letter to check the weight: the scale balanced, the seal numbers matched the register, and after they counted through No. 3 hold section by section, what was stacked there was ballast stone. The face of the man leading them had nowhere to go; when he tried to quietly fold the letter away, I pressed down on his hand: "Black words on white paper, with a signature set to it. Please file it in the case record. From now on, Luoxia Customs will vouch for the Yunque; this letter is the guarantee." He left faster than he had come.
When Liu Chengye's fragrant cakes had been delivered and settled, he stood outside the crowd and bowed deeply to me. I waved my hand: "Goods clear, accounts clear. If you use the Yunque in the future, the price stays the same." His eyes reddened for a moment, and he did not say a word. That was best. Some things need not be spoken through; speaking them through only makes people feel estranged.
Yi-11 was the last to disembark. Zhou Shun stopped at the gangway entrance and bent at the waist all the way down, lower than any time before. I said only one sentence: "The bunk has been withdrawn. From now on, that berth is reserved for people who sleep heavily." He straightened and left; this time his heels touched the ground, one sound with every step.
The chen hour. Teahouse. The table by the window.
A blue-gray straight robe; a pair of hands kept exceedingly well, the nails trimmed round and smooth. That length of silver chain in the rain ten years ago had now been replaced with a more respectable pendant. Steward Shen rose to offer tea, the smile lines folding with perfect evenness: "Captain Su Si. Luoxia's pre-rain—"
He was not the one pouring the tea.
Hou San came up with the pot, filled it to seventy percent, and did not spill a drop. The instant he drew back the spout, the old calluses at the web of his thumb pressed against the pot handle, and a tendon on the back of his hand jumped finely.
"Hou San, do those hands of yours still shake?" I took the note from the pocket against my chest and set it beside the teacup. "If they shake, that's right. It means you still remember the Cable Gang's rules."
The perfectly even folds of Steward Shen's smile paused for half a breath.
"Rules are good things." I did not touch the tea; first I looked at the hand that had poured it. The spaces between the fingers were clean, with no blue-gray ash. It shook, and shook honestly. "The Cable Gang recognizes knots, not words. The merchants' guild probably recognizes seals, not people. The crane-character seal—there are only two people in the Yungang branch who dare set it. The guild head is at the head office a thousand li away. The other one," I pushed the note half an inch toward him, "is also lying in Customs' case record this morning."
He placed two fingers on the note but did not open it. "What does Captain Su Si wish to discuss?"
"An accounting. You remember it."
"Ten years ago, before the fire started in the back alley behind the Dan Firm, a sum for the cargo first passed through your hands. The fire had not started, but the money was ready. Someone has been keeping that item on my behalf."
"That night, the tarpaulin soaked through with tung oil; the person who, in the rain, carried no umbrella, timed the heat, and walked to the alley mouth; the silver chain at the cuff—someone has been keeping that item on my behalf as well."
"At Yungang Dock, the raw dregs falsely using Baicaotang's name—the man is still in Lao Cai's hands, and his mouth is very steady. Remember that."
"The added weight in No. 3 hold, the broken ladder on the outer hull, the pigeon letter sent three days ahead—this item," I lifted my chin toward Hou San, "was also recorded by those shaking hands."
Outside the window, the first gong of Luoxia opening for business drifted over from afar. Half a cup of tea had gone cool.
"The account is finished." I picked up the cup Hou San had poured and took a sip. It was hot. The hand was clean, so I would touch it. "Two conclusions. First, the favor I owed Xuanhe—the principal was false, the fire was lit by you, and the money was prepared by you. A false account need not be repaid; that is only right and proper. Second, I copied out this ledger once. The crane-character seal at the head office is larger than this one of mine. Whenever you want the guild head to verify it, I will deliver it."
Steward Shen was silent for a long time. Luoxia's sun climbed in through the window lattice and shone on those hands of his, kept so exceedingly well.
"Su Wanxing." For the first time, he called me by my full name. "Ten years ago, I said this fish was worth raising."
"Pity you set the wrong hook." I rose, drew the note back from beneath his fingers, and pressed the tea money under the bowl. This cup I paid for myself. "A fish born from cable workers recognizes rope, not bait. What is tied in the rope is a dead knot; the harder you struggle, the tighter it gets."
"The Yunque's next run will call at Yungang as usual. Xuanhe will still receive Liu Chengye's goods as usual. The merchants' guild is the merchants' guild; you are you. I can tell this account apart. But if anyone climbs my outer hull again," I stopped at the doorway and did not look back, "my skill at cutting cables has not rusted in ten years."
When I went downstairs, Hou San chased after me two steps and counted out the half-jin's worth of wine money into my palm, coin by coin. The copper coins were warm. He had carried them for ten years and warmed them through.
"And the interest?"
"The interest is," he lowered his voice and pointed upstairs, "just now, while you were reciting the account, his left hand kept pressing down on the tea tray. Pressing it down, not daring to turn it over. Whatever was under the tea tray, I did not see it. You did not see it either."
I weighed that handful of copper coins and put them into my sleeve pocket. At noon I delivered that star-blue ash to Lao Cai, kept the note close against my body, and in my sleeve pocket there was only the wine money left, pressed against my wrist, warm.
Under heaven there are great piles of true accounts and false accounts. The only thing warmed through is this one handful.
At the dock, the Yunque was berthed neat and true. Gecko was leaning against a cable post and lifted his severed finger toward me—he had stayed, and the outer hull on the next run would still be his post. Uncle Mute stood in the shadow of the hatch and signed the character "clear" to me. I nodded: hold clear, accounts clear, people clear too.
The wind-window from Luoxia to Yungang opened in the wei hour; there was still plenty of time. I returned to my old place at the gangway entrance and turned the register to a new page.
"Yunque, departing Luoxia—hold your tags high, luggage stays with people, those with children board first!"
The wind came from the far side of the cloud sea, steady. This voyage had flown true.
